back: The client sends an HTTP request every few seconds. The server responds immediately, with data or empty. Simple but wasteful.
Average delay = half the polling interval. A 10-second interval means 5 seconds average delay.
The client sends a request. The server holds it open until data is available (or timeout). Then the client immediately re-requests.
Long polling delivers updates near-instantly (no interval delay) and avoids empty responses. But it holds connections on the server.
A long-lived HTTP connection where the server pushes text events. Browser API: new EventSource('/events'). Auto-reconnects with Last-Event-ID.
Server-to-client only (half-duplex). Text only (no binary). Limited to 6 connections per domain in HTTP/1.1.

front: How does a WebSocket connection start?
back: HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket header. Server responds 101 Switching Protocols. Connection becomes full-duplex WebSocket.
Full-duplex, low per-message overhead (2–14 bytes framing), binary and text support, near-zero latency.
Stateful (tied to one server), no auto-reconnect, proxy/firewall issues, high memory at scale.

front: How to scale WebSockets across servers?
back: Multiple connection servers + pub/sub bus (Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, NATS). Publish to the bus; subscribed servers push to their clients.
Periodic ping/pong frames to detect dead connections (client lost network, NAT timeout). Missed heartbeat → close connection.

front: When to use SSE vs WebSockets?
back: SSE: server-to-client only (notifications, feeds, dashboards). WebSockets: bidirectional (chat, collaboration, gaming).
Each WebSocket connection uses one file descriptor. Linux default is ~1024; tuned to ~1M. Monitor and scale horizontally.
Low-frequency updates where latency is not critical: email check every 30s, dashboard refresh every minute.
Full-duplex: both sides send at any time (WebSocket). Half-duplex: only one side sends at a time (SSE: server only).

front: What is a reconnect storm, and how do you prevent it?
back: When a connection server dies, all its clients reconnect at once and flood the fleet and auth service. Clients use exponential backoff with random jitter to spread the reconnects out.

front: Polling QPS for N users polling every T seconds?
back: N ÷ T. 10 million users every 3 s ≈ 3.3 million requests per second, mostly empty.
